Biochemistry L5 · 3 sections

Diet fat and coronary heart disease

Biochemistry L5 · 1

Blood lipids and coronary heart disease

How it works

Cholesterol travels in blood packed in lipoproteins. LDL carries it to tissues and raises coronary risk; HDL is associated with lower risk. Lowering LDL by diet or drugs lowers risk.

What to do first

  1. Encourage diet control and expect a 10-20% fall; expect 30-40% with statins.
  2. Read a high HDL as protective.

Client example

A client with high LDL asks whether diet alone is enough: it lowers LDL by about 10-20%.

Common trap

Treating all cholesterol as bad: high HDL lowers risk.

Memory trick

LDL = Lousy, HDL = Helpful.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Elevated cholesterol increases the risk of CHD.

Key ideas

  • Total blood cholesterol comes from diet and endogenous synthesis and is carried by lipoproteins, especially LDL and HDL.
  • CHD risk rises with total and LDL cholesterol; high HDL-cholesterol is associated with decreased risk.
  • Diet control lowers TC and LDL-C by 10-20%; statins lower them by 30-40%.

Source: Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD)

Biochemistry L5 · 2

Types of dietary fat and their effects

How it works

A fat's effect depends on its fatty acids: saturation, the number and position of double bonds, and cis or trans shape. Omega numbers count from the methyl end to the first double bond.

What to do first

  1. Advise limiting saturated and trans fats.
  2. Suggest olive oil (MUFA) and fatty fish (omega-3).
  3. Teach the label clue "partially hydrogenated".

Client example

A client switches butter for olive oil: LDL falls and HDL rises.

Common trap

Thinking omega-3 mainly lowers LDL; its main effect is on triacylglycerol, arrhythmia, thrombosis and inflammation.

Memory trick

SMASH fish for omega-3: salmon, mackerel, anchovies, sardines, herring.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Trans fats should be under of energy (under 2.2 g per day on 2000 kcal).
  • EPA has carbons and 5 double bonds; DHA has 22 carbons and 6.

Key ideas

  • Saturated fats (no double bonds; dairy, meat, coconut and palm oils) raise TC and LDL-C and CHD risk.
  • Monounsaturated fats (one double bond; olive oil, oleic acid, omega-9) lower TC and LDL-C and raise HDL-C when substituted for saturated fats.
  • Omega-6 fats (first double bond at carbon 6 from the methyl end; corn, sesame, cottonseed, sunflower oils) lower TC and LDL-C but also lower HDL-C and are proinflammatory.
  • Omega-3 fats suppress arrhythmia, reduce blood triacylglycerol, decrease thrombosis and inflammation, with little effect on LDL-C and HDL-C.
  • Trans fats are chemically unsaturated but behave like saturated fats: they raise LDL-C and lower HDL-C; formed by partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils (margarine).

Source: Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD)

Biochemistry L5 · 3

Dietary cholesterol, plant sterols and cholesterol-lowering factors

How it works

Dietary cholesterol matters less than the fat mix. Plant sterols compete with cholesterol in the gut, so less is absorbed and LDL falls.

What to do first

  1. Correct a client who focuses only on dietary cholesterol.
  2. Suggest plant-sterol margarines, fiber and MUFA.

Client example

A client says eaten cholesterol matters more than fat type: needs further teaching.

Common trap

Thinking plant foods contain cholesterol.

Memory trick

Cholesterol only comes with a face (animal products).

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Plant sterols reduce LDL by inhibiting intestinal of cholesterol.

Key ideas

  • Dietary cholesterol is found only in animal products; its effect on blood cholesterol is less important than the amount and type of fatty acids.
  • Plant sterols reduce LDL-cholesterol by inhibiting intestinal absorption of cholesterol.
  • Dietary factors that decrease blood cholesterol: omega-6 PUFA, MUFA, antioxidants (beta carotene, vitamins E and C), plant sterols, vegetable fiber, large-dose vitamin B3.

Source: Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD)

Biochemistry L6 · 3 sections

Oxidative stress and atherosclerosis

Biochemistry L6 · 1

Free radicals, ROS and RNS

How it works

A free radical has an unpaired outer electron and steals one from the nearest molecule, starting chain damage to lipids, proteins and DNA. Non-radicals have no unpaired electron but are strong oxidants. Damage occurs when oxidants outrun antioxidants.

What to do first

  1. Classify each species as radical or non-radical.
  2. Separate endogenous (metabolism, phagocytosis) from exogenous (drugs, radiation, smoke) sources.

Client example

A smoker has an exogenous source of free radicals in cigarette smoke.

Common trap

Calling H2O2 a radical.

Memory trick

Radicals end with a dot: O2.-, OH., NO.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Peroxynitrite is a reactive nitrogen .

Key ideas

  • Oxidative stress: an imbalance favoring oxidants and/or disfavoring antioxidants, potentially leading to damage.
  • A free radical is a molecule with an unpaired electron in an outer valence shell; it plucks an electron from the nearest molecule.
  • ROS radicals: superoxide, hydroxyl, peroxyl. ROS non-radicals: hydrogen peroxide, hypochlorous acid, ozone.
  • RNS radicals: nitric oxide, nitrogen dioxide. RNS non-radical: peroxynitrite.
  • Endogenous sources: electron leak from the respiratory chain, oxidases (xanthine oxidase), prostaglandin synthesis, NO from arginine, phagocytosis. Exogenous: drug metabolism (halothane, cytochrome P450), ionizing radiation, cigarette smoke.

Source: Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress)

Biochemistry L6 · 2

Respiratory burst, nitric oxide and antioxidants

How it works

Reactive species are also tools. Neutrophils make superoxide, H2O2 and hypochlorous acid to kill bacteria. Endothelial NO dilates vessels. Antioxidant enzymes and nutrients keep the balance.

What to do first

  1. Link sepsis and inflammation to large iNOS output.
  2. Explain nitroglycerin works by becoming NO.

Client example

A client's angina is relieved by nitroglycerin, which is metabolized to nitric oxide.

Common trap

Mixing up constitutive eNOS (low, steady) with inducible iNOS (large, prolonged).

Memory trick

i for inducible and inflammatory.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • The enzyme that converts H2O2 and chloride into hypochlorous acid is .
  • NO synthase uses as its precursor.

Key ideas

  • Respiratory burst: NADPH oxidase converts O2 to superoxide; superoxide dismutase makes H2O2; myeloperoxidase converts H2O2 and chloride to hypochlorous acid, which kills bacteria.
  • NO is a free radical gas with a half-life of seconds, made from L-arginine by NO synthase.
  • eNOS and nNOS are constitutive and make low levels of NO; iNOS (macrophages, neutrophils; induced by bacterial toxins, TNF, cytokines) makes large amounts for hours or days.
  • eNOS-derived NO improves vascular dilation and perfusion; nitroglycerin is metabolized to NO and relieves coronary spasm in angina.
  • Enzymatic antioxidants: superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase. Nutrient antioxidants: vitamins A, E, C, selenium. Metabolic: glutathione, ceruloplasmin, albumin, transferrin, ferritin, uric acid.

Source: Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress)

Biochemistry L6 · 3

Oxidized LDL and the stages of atherosclerosis

How it works

Oxidation turns LDL into a danger signal. Oxidized LDL in the intima activates endothelium to recruit monocytes; macrophages take it up by scavenger receptors and become foam cells. Smooth muscle cells build a cap, dead cells pile up into a necrotic core, and a vulnerable plaque can rupture.

What to do first

  1. Trace the stages in order from endothelial dysfunction to thrombosis.
  2. Link impaired efferocytosis to the necrotic core.

Client example

A client's plaque ruptures and exposes thrombogenic material, causing an MI.

Common trap

Thinking VCAM-1 is on macrophages; it is on activated endothelial cells.

Memory trick

Dysfunction, Oxidation, Recruitment, Foam, Cap, Core, Clot.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Monocytes are captured by and ICAM-1 on activated endothelium.

Key ideas

  • Free radicals oxidize LDL cholesterol; oxidized LDL triggers inflammation and plaque buildup.
  • Stages: endothelial dysfunction, LDL retention and oxidation in the intima, recruitment of monocytes and T cells by VCAM-1, ICAM-1 and MCP-1, foam cell formation (fatty streak), SMC migration and fibrous cap, necrotic core and calcification, rupture or erosion with thrombosis.
  • Macrophages engulf oxidized LDL via scavenger receptors and become lipid-laden foam cells.
  • Failure to clear dead macrophages and SMCs (impaired efferocytosis) enlarges an acellular necrotic core.

Source: Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress)

Biochemistry past papers · 2 sections

Lipoproteins and eicosanoids (past papers)

Biochemistry past papers · 1

Lipoproteins and cholesterol metabolism (past papers)

How it works

Lipoproteins carry fat in the blood: the intestine makes chylomicrons (apo B-48) and the liver makes VLDL (apo B-100). HDL donates apo C-II and apo E to them; apo C-II activates lipoprotein lipase to unload triglyceride, and apo A-I activates LCAT to esterify cholesterol on HDL. Cholesterol synthesis is controlled at HMG CoA reductase (activated by insulin, blocked by statins), and cholesterol leaves the body as bile acids. Your uploaded lectures do not cover this; the facts come from the past-paper keys.

What to do first

  1. Match each apo to its job: B-100 VLDL structure, B-48 chylomicron, C-II activates LPL, A-I activates LCAT.
  2. Hypothyroidism with high cholesterol: less conversion to bile acids.
  3. Fatty liver: triglyceride made faster than VLDL can export it.

Client example

A client with Tangier disease has orange tonsils and a very low HDL.

Common trap

Mixing up apo B-100 (VLDL, LDL) and apo B-48 (chylomicrons).

Memory trick

B-48 is the Bowel's apo; B-100 is the liver's full-length one.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Apo C-II activates .
  • Abetalipoproteinemia lowers both and chylomicrons.

Key ideas

  • Statins competitively inhibit HMG CoA reductase, the enzyme insulin activates in the fed state.
  • In hypothyroidism cholesterol is high because conversion of cholesterol to bile acids is impaired.
  • Apo B-100 is the structural apolipoprotein of VLDL; nascent chylomicrons and VLDL get apo C-II and apo E from HDL.
  • Apo C-II activates lipoprotein lipase; apo A-I activates LCAT, which converts free cholesterol to cholesterol esters.
  • Fatty liver: the liver makes more triglyceride than it can export as VLDL.
  • Tangier disease: low HDL. Abetalipoproteinemia: decreased VLDL and chylomicrons.

Source: Shams Practices QB (past papers); not in your uploaded slides

Biochemistry past papers · 2

Eicosanoids: COX-2 and prostacyclin (past papers)

How it works

Eicosanoids are made from fatty acids. COX-2 is induced in inflammation and makes inflammatory prostaglandins; prostacyclin (PGI2) from the vessel wall dilates vessels. Your slides list prostaglandin synthesis as a source of free radicals; the rest comes from the past-paper keys.

What to do first

  1. Link COX-2 to inflammation and PGI2 to vasodilation.

Client example

A question on the enzyme behind inflammatory prostaglandins: COX-2.

Common trap

Calling PGI2 a promoter of platelet aggregation; that is thromboxane A2.

Memory trick

PGI2 = Protects (dilates, stops platelets).

Test yourself tap each blank

  • PGI2 is a .

Key ideas

  • COX-2 makes the prostaglandins of the inflammatory response.
  • Prostacyclin (PGI2) is a vasodilator.

Source: Shams Practices QB (past papers); not in your uploaded slides

Read me

This exam has two pages that work as one system: the Drill finds what you do not know and proves when you do, and the Mastery Guide teaches it again. Every fact on a Fix my misses card in the Drill is in the Guide section it links to.

How to use the Drill

  1. Start with the pre-test. It asks 3 questions from every topic and gives each topic a level: Strong (80% and up), Okay (60-79%) or Weak (under 60%). It never uses last-pass questions, so those stay fresh.
  2. Or go lecture by lecture. The "By lecture" card gives every lecture its own pre-test (up to 8 questions), its own last pass, a level, and a Guide button that opens only that lecture's sections.
  3. Think first. Each question appears without its choices for 10-15 seconds. Answer it in your head before the choices show up. Turn the timer off on any question if you need to.
  4. Be honest after a right answer. Choose "Knew it" or "I guessed" (key G). A guess comes back sooner.
  5. Read the "why" on every miss. You get why your pick is wrong, the key idea and the concept card. A different question on the same concept follows 3-6 questions later.
  6. Use short daily sessions. Pick 20 questions or a 30-minute timed plan. Questions you just answered rest before they come back, so each session is new work.
  7. Finish with the last pass. It asks every question from the cases asked in class, the slide exercises and the facts flagged on slides, shakiest first.

Keys: 1-6 pick an option, Enter checks and moves on, S stars, G marks a guess. Progress saves on this device and, inside claude.ai, to your account so your phone, tablet and laptop share it.

How to use the Mastery Guide

  1. Use the lecture bar at the top to show one lecture at a time, or "All lectures" for everything.
  2. Read a section in order: how it works, what to do first, the client example, the common trap and the memory trick.
  3. Cover the page and tap each blank in "Test yourself" only after you have said the answer.
  4. Finish each section by reading the Key ideas box. Those lines are exactly what the Drill's concept cards show.

How to use both together

  1. Drill to find: run the pre-test, then open Fix my misses to see the concepts you keep missing.
  2. Guide to re-learn: follow the card's "Open in the guide" link and study that section.
  3. Drill to prove: come back and press "Fix this". A question counts as solid only after you get it right twice in a row (three times for true/false), with rest between.
